exp.w: How many UFC fights fall inside this window.
exp.y: Every rate on this page is built out of these fights. Three is where a profile starts to mean something; ten is where it stops moving much.

exp.w: Total minutes fought in the window.
exp.y: A fighter who finishes everyone in ninety seconds has very little cage time, and every per-minute rate of his is built on a thin sample. This is the denominator of the page.

exp.w: Average length of his fights, in minutes.
exp.y: Short fights mean finishes — his or his opponent's. Long fights mean decisions. The number tells you what kind of night he usually has.

exp.w: UFC fights per calendar year, from his first fight in the window to his last.
exp.y: Activity is a skill too. Long layoffs come with ring rust and lost prime years.
exp.f: fights ÷ years spanned (at least one year)

exp.w: Share of his UFC fights in the window that he won.
exp.y: The record is the thing everyone starts from. Everything below is an attempt to explain it.

exp.w: An Elo rating, computed across every UFC fight in order, read at the end of the window. 1500 is a debutant; finishes move it more than decisions.
exp.y: A record says how often he won. A rating says who he beat. Beating a 1700 is worth far more than beating a 1400, and the rating knows the difference when the record does not.
exp.f: K = 32, ×1.25 for a finish, expected score from the rating gap

exp.w: The average Elo rating of the opponents he faced in the window, as they were on fight night.
exp.y: Strength of schedule. Two fighters with identical striking numbers have not done the same thing if one did it against contenders and the other against debutants.

exp.w: Significant strikes he lands per minute of cage time. "Significant" is every strike at distance, plus power strikes in the clinch and on the ground.
exp.y: Volume. The single most-watched striking number in the sport, and the one the judges see most clearly.

exp.w: Significant strikes his opponents land on him per minute.
exp.y: The other half of every striking exchange. A high number is a fighter who gets hit — through poor defense, or because his style invites the trade.

exp.w: Significant strikes landed minus significant strikes absorbed, per minute.
exp.y: The number analysts reach for first. A positive differential wins rounds; a large one wins fights. It rolls output and defense into one reading.

exp.w: Significant strikes landed by both men combined, per minute.
exp.y: What kind of fight he is in. Some fighters drag every opponent into a brawl; some make every fight a chess match. Neither is better, but it tells you how to read his other numbers.

exp.w: Share of his significant strike attempts that landed.
exp.y: Precision. High-accuracy fighters pick shots; low-accuracy fighters throw volume and accept the misses. Read it next to pace.

exp.w: Share of opponents' significant strike attempts that did not land.
exp.y: Head movement, footwork, range. The best defensive strikers make the other man miss six of every ten.

exp.w: Knockdowns scored per fifteen minutes — the length of a three-round fight.
exp.y: Power, and the ability to land it. Knockdowns end fights and swing rounds; they are also the most weight-class-dependent number on the page, which is why the ranking is within his division.

exp.w: Knockdowns per hundred significant strikes landed.
exp.y: Power per punch, separated from volume. A fighter who lands little but drops people has a very different weapon from one who lands a lot and drops people.

exp.w: Times he was knocked down, per fifteen minutes.
exp.y: Chin, and defense against the big shot. Fighters who get dropped often get finished eventually.

exp.w: Share of his landed significant strikes that went to the head.
exp.y: Around four in five UFC strikes go to the head, so this is mostly a stylistic signature: a low head share is a body-and-leg fighter.
exp.f: head strikes landed ÷ sig. strikes landed

exp.w: Share of his landed significant strikes that went to the body.
exp.y: Body work is slow-acting and under-scored, which is why fighters who invest in it tend to be the ones who finish late.

exp.w: Share of his landed significant strikes that went to the legs.
exp.y: Leg kicks compound. A high share here is a fighter who wins the second half of fights by taking the other man's base away in the first.

exp.w: Share of his landed significant strikes thrown at distance — on the feet, out of the clinch.
exp.y: Where he does his work. A pure striker lives here; a wrestler lands most of his on the ground.

exp.w: Share of his landed significant strikes thrown in the clinch.
exp.y: Knees, elbows, dirty boxing. The clinch is where strength and cage craft show up in the striking numbers.

exp.w: Share of his landed significant strikes thrown on the ground.
exp.y: Ground and pound. Read it with control time — a fighter who gets on top and stays there lands most of his best shots from there.

exp.w: Takedowns landed per fifteen minutes.
exp.y: Whether he can put the fight where he wants it. The average UFC fighter lands about one and a half per fifteen; a wrestler lands four or five.

exp.w: Share of his takedown attempts that succeeded.
exp.y: The league average sits under forty percent. A fighter who shoots and fails is spending energy and eating knees for nothing.

exp.w: Share of opponents' takedown attempts that he stuffed.
exp.y: For a striker this is the most important grappling number there is: it decides whether he gets to fight his fight. For a wrestler it decides whether he can fight from the top rather than the bottom.

exp.w: Minutes of ground or clinch control per fifteen minutes fought. Control is time spent in a dominant position — on top, or pressing the opponent against the fence.
exp.y: Judges reward control, and it is the surest way to win a round without landing a big shot. Not tracked before 2000, so fighters from the early era have no bar here.

exp.w: His control time minus his opponents' control time, per fifteen minutes.
exp.y: Who was on top. A fighter with a lot of control time who also gets controlled a lot is in a grappling war; a positive differential is a fighter who dictates position.

exp.w: Minutes his opponents spent controlling him, per fifteen.
exp.y: Time spent on your back is time not spent winning. This is the grappling equivalent of strikes absorbed.

exp.w: Submission attempts per fifteen minutes.
exp.y: How often he hunts for a finish on the ground. Attempts, not finishes — a fighter who threatens keeps the other man honest even when nothing lands.

exp.w: Times he reversed position — got off his back and onto top — per fifteen minutes.
exp.y: Scrambling. The fighters who can't be held down make wrestlers' control time worthless.

exp.w: Share of his wins that came by knockout or submission rather than the judges.
exp.y: Finishers get title shots and bonuses. A high finish rate is a fighter who does not leave it to three people at cageside.

exp.w: Share of his fights that ended with him winning by knockout or TKO.
exp.y: The most direct measure of fight-ending power there is.

exp.w: Share of his fights that ended with him winning by submission.
exp.y: Jiu-jitsu that closes. Attempts are in the grappling panel; this is the ones that worked.

exp.w: Share of his fights that he finished inside the first round.
exp.y: Fast starters. Also a fighter whose whole game may be built for five minutes — read it with the round curve below.

exp.w: Share of his fights that he lost by knockout or submission.
exp.y: Getting finished is the loss that follows a fighter. A high number is a fighter who, when he loses, loses badly.

exp.w: Times he was knocked out or stopped by strikes, per hundred significant strikes absorbed.
exp.y: Chin, adjusted for how much he gets hit. A fighter who absorbs a lot and never goes out is durable; one who goes out early and often is not, whatever his defense says.

exp.w: Share of his fights that went to the judges.
exp.y: Context, not skill. A fighter who never sees the scorecards fights very differently from one who lives there.

exp.w: Significant strikes landed per minute in first rounds.
exp.y: How he starts. Read against his later rounds, not against other fighters' first rounds.

exp.w: Significant strikes landed per minute in second rounds.
exp.y: The middle of the fight, where conditioning starts to tell.

exp.w: Significant strikes landed per minute in third rounds.
exp.y: How he closes. Championship rounds are excluded so five-round fighters are not compared on a different footing.

exp.w: His third-round output per minute divided by his first-round output per minute. Above 1 is a fighter who gets stronger; below 1 is a fighter who fades.
exp.y: Cardio and pacing in one number. Some of the best finishers in the sport are below 1 here — they front-load on purpose — so read it with his finish rate.
exp.f: R3 sig. strikes/min ÷ R1 sig. strikes/min

exp.w: Significant strikes absorbed per minute in third rounds.
exp.y: Whether the other man is still landing on him late. Tired fighters get hit.
